Sensitivities and Hessians

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-sensitivities.Rmd
methods-sensitivities.Rmd

The derivatives of the objective come from the sensitivities of the ODE solution and the chain rule through every function object, without finite differences. Guide: Sensitivities; integrators: cppDE.

sweep returns
forward gradient, Gauss-Newton Hessian
forward over forward exact Hessian
reverse gradient
forward over reverse exact Hessian

Forward sensitivities

The sensitivities \(S = \partial x / \partial \theta\) of \(\dot x = f(x, \theta)\), \(x(t_0) = x_0(\theta)\), solve

\[\dot S = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, S + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}, \qquad S(t_0) = \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}, \tag{1}\]

\(n_x n_\theta\) further equations. cppDE evaluates \(f\) on dual numbers, one tangent per parameter, and steps states and tangents together. The step-size control includes the tangents (sensErrCon), so the sensitivities are as accurate as the states (forward sensitivities). An event passes the tangents through the saltation matrix of the jump (events). Every further function object of g*x*p multiplies by the Jacobian of that object, e.g. \(g_x S + g_\theta\) for \(y = g(x, \theta)\).

Gradient and Hessian of the objective

Each data point adds, up to a constant,

\[\ell_j = r_j^2 + \log \sigma_j^2, \qquad r_j = \frac{f_j - y_j}{\sigma_j}, \tag{2}\]

the summand of the data term. For fixed \(\sigma_j\) and \(J = \partial r / \partial \theta\), the gradient is \(2 J^\top r\) and the Hessian

\[\nabla^2 \sum_j r_j^2 = 2 J^\top J + 2 \sum_j r_j\, \nabla^2 r_j . \tag{3}\]

The Gauss-Newton term \(2 J^\top J\) is positive semidefinite and needs first-order sensitivities; the second term matters for large residuals or strong nonlinearity.

Gauss-Newton with an error model

For \(\sigma_j(\theta)\), the Hessian of \(\ell_j\) in \((f_j, \sigma_j)\) is

\[L_j = \frac{2}{\sigma_j^2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 r_j \\ -2 r_j & 3 r_j^2 - 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det L_j = -\frac{4\,(1 + r_j^2)}{\sigma_j^4} < 0. \tag{4}\]

The Gauss-Newton Hessian of normL2() is \(\sum_j J_j^\top L_j J_j\), \(J_j\) the Jacobian of \((f_j, \sigma_j)\): exact curvature of \(\ell_j\), no second derivatives of \(f_j\) and \(\sigma_j\). The concave \(\log \sigma_j^2\) gives \(L_j\) one negative eigenvalue, so the matrix is in general indefinite along directions that move a sigma where residuals are small. The exact Hessian adds the second derivatives of \(f_j\) and \(\sigma_j\), weighted by \(2 r_j / \sigma_j\) and \(2 (1 - r_j^2) / \sigma_j\).

Forward over forward

Differentiating (1) again gives \(n_x n_\theta (n_\theta + 1) / 2\) equations and the exact Hessian, for small models.

Reverse sweep

The gradient of the objective alone follows from one backward sweep with the multipliers \(\lambda(t)\) and the data term \(\ell\),

\[\dot\lambda = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top} \lambda - \left(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}(-2 \log L)}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \int \lambda^\top \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\, \mathrm{d}t + \dots, \tag{5}\]

with jumps of \(\lambda\) at the measurement times. cppDE uses the discrete adjoint of the integrator steps, the exact derivative of the computed objective, with checkpoints of the forward trajectory (reverse mode). The cost is a few times the value, independent of \(n_\theta\). The value pass solves without sensitivities, and the sweep uses the step grid of that pass. Pimpl() passes the sweep through the Jacobian of the root (Steady states).

Accuracy of a reverse gradient

By default the adjoint follows the step grid of the states without error control.

option of optionsReverse effect
refine = TRUE every step held to the CVODES backward error test under the solve tolerances; a failing step is swept again in substeps
gradtol the share of each step in the gradient added to that test as absolute tolerance

A trust region converges with a gradient accurate relative to the gradient size [1], [2], so gradtol is a fraction of the gradient scale (checking the sweep).

A refined sweep differentiates the trajectory with substeps, not the computed one. Under refine it therefore returns, per seed, the first-order change of the seeded functional between the two: over the steps, the adjoint at the step end times the difference of the end states, plus the seeds times the difference of the observed values (value correction). The normL2() seed gives the change of the objective, a second seed the change of chi2. The reverse objective adds both, so value and gradient belong to one function, and a value-only call also sweeps. The corrected value is not necessarily closer to the exact one; accepted steps get no correction.

Forward over reverse

Forward tangents, one per parameter, ride on the backward sweep, which returns one Hessian column per tangent. Cost grows like a forward solve; nothing of order \(n_\theta^2\) is integrated or stored (forward over reverse).

Second derivatives along directions

FOCEI (Nonlinear mixed-effects models) needs traces \(\operatorname{tr}(M\, \partial H_i / \partial \psi)\) for the volume term and the joint Hessian along random-effect directions. Random effects of different groups never share a condition, so the \(k\)-th random effect of all groups shares one tangent \(v_k\), and one forward pass along \(K\) tangents serves all groups. A backward sweep with seed \(w\) on the predictions and sigmas of the data rows, and \(\dot w_k\) along tangent \(k\), returns \(J^\top w\) and

\[\sum_r w_r\, \nabla^2 f_r\, v_k + J^\top \dot w_k \tag{6}\]

for every \(k\), \(f_r\) prediction or sigma of row \(r\), \(J\) their Jacobian. With the gradient of the row loss as seed and \(L_r J_r v_k\) as tangent derivative, \(L_r\) the Hessian (4), the sweep gives \(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta}\), \(\Phi_i^{\eta\psi}\) and the mode shift \(\mathrm{d}\hat\eta / \mathrm{d}\psi = -(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi}\). The trace gradients are linear in \(M\): seed \(j\) is \(2 L_r J_{r,j}\), with tangent derivative the derivative of \(L_r\) contracted with \(J_{r,j}\) and \(J_{r,k}\). With \(U_{jk}\) slice \(k\) of the result for seed \(j\),

\[\nabla \operatorname{tr}(M H_i) = \sum_{j,k} M_{jk}\, U_{jk} \tag{7}\]

for every symmetric \(M\): \(K\) seeds for any number of matrices. Hessian rows and trace seeds go back in one sweep, every cotangent with \(K + 1\) blocks, the seed and the derivative of the seed along each tangent.
